newsitem.title: CANADA: Oxy involvement seen unlikely in Sudan oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Oxy involvement seen unlikely in Sudan oil deal.

text.p: Occidental Petroleum Corp. is seen as unlikely to be involved in a Sudanese oil deal expected to be announced shortly by Canada's International Petroleum Corp..
"I think it's almost a certainty (that Occidental will not be in the deal)," a well-placed source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said on Monday.

IPC Chairman Adolf Lundin told Reuters in Stockholm last week that a deal would be announced imminently to develop the much-watched concession, near a tract operated by an international consortium including Arakis Energy Corp.

Several industry sources close to the Sudan deals had said Occidental -- which was earlier reported negotiating for a stake in the $1 billion Arakis transaction before being ejected from the talks by the Sudan government -- was mulling a deal with IPC.

But over the past week, the prospect of Occidental's involvement in the new concession appeared to diminish, with the company reportedly deciding to forego the deal because of its less-certain nature.
"It's possible...it's very much in flux," IPC director Lukas Lundin said in a phone interview from Vancouver last week.
As has been the case since speculation about Occidental's involvement in Sudan began to surface last summer, officials with the Los Angeles-based firm declined comment.

Lundin said IPC, which also lobbied for a stake in the Arakis project, remained keen on oil exploration in the strife-torn African nation after the final consortium participants were chosen to include the state oil companies of China and Malaysia and the Khartoum government.
"As we got blown out of the water on that one, they said maybe you can have this," he said.
Analysts have said the alternative lands located southeast of Arakis's Heglig and Unity fields were far less proven geologically after only one well was drilled several years ago.
The Arakis concession, meanwhile, was estimated by ex-operator Chevron Corp. to harbor as much as 3.5 billion barrels, and several major discoveries have been made since Arakis began drilling there.
The difference between the two concessions in scale and proven reserves was seen as a possible reason behind Occidental's abandoning a deal with IPC.
Occidental risked further political fallout because of the strained relationship between Sudan and the United States.
Sudan was named under Washington's Anti-terrorism Act, which sanctioned seven nations it accused of supporting international terrorism.
But Sudan was not subject to the broad sanctions placed on five other nations under the law, which left a window open for an oil deal to be negotiated by a U.S. firm.

"This Arakis concession helps you understand why Oxy might want to do one and not the other," said Kirk Dornbush, president of Atlanta-based fund management company Diem Investments, which follows both Arakis and IPC closely.
"This...concession is considered one of the world's last great concessions. One can take an awful lot of heat to develop that. But to go in and do a rank wildcat and basically take the same heat?"
The Arakis consortium plans to develop the two fields and build a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea from southern Sudan by 1999.
